blocks.text: This unit explores methods to find the maximum and minimum values of quadratic functions using completing the square and graphical analysis. It also covers the inverse of quadratic functions, determining their domain and range. Additionally, students will learn to solve absolute value quadratic equations and inequalities, as well as equations of rational, radical and exponential forms that can be reduced to quadratic equations. Finally, the unit demonstrates the practical applications of quadratic equations and inequalities in solving real-world problems, providing a strong foundation for problem-solving and analysis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The introduction also mentions equations of "exponential" form. The sections of this unit (3.4.1 and 3.4.2) only treat rational and radical equations; there is no separate section or example on exponential equations in this unit.

blocks.title: About this unit
blocks.text:
What this unit is about: a quadratic function \(f(x) = ax^{2} + bx + c\) describes many curved paths and many "best value" questions: the highest point of a thrown ball, the largest area of a fence, the lowest cost. Unit 3 studies its graph (the parabola), its highest or lowest value, its inverse, and equations and inequalities built from it.
What you will learn: sketching a quadratic function and reading its vertex, intercepts and increasing/decreasing intervals (3.1.1); finding the maximum or minimum value by completing the square (3.1.2); the inverse of a quadratic function with its domain and range (3.2); absolute value quadratic equations and inequalities (3.3); rational and radical equations that reduce to quadratics (3.4); and real-world problems (3.5).
What you should already know: solving a quadratic equation by factorization and by the quadratic formula \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\); plotting points on the coordinate plane; the ideas of domain, range, one-to-one and inverse function from Unit 2; interval notation such as \([2, \infty)\) and \((-1, 7)\).
A quadratic function is a polynomial function of degree two. It is typically expressed in the standard form:

blocks.text_alt: f of x equals a x squared plus b x plus c

blocks.text: where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are real numbers, and \(a \ne 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Degree two" means the highest power of \(x\) is 2. The three numbers have names:
\(a\) is the leading coefficient (the number with \(x^{2}\)),
\(b\) is the coefficient of \(x\),
\(c\) is the constant term.
Why \(a \ne 0\)? If \(a = 0\), the \(x^{2}\) term disappears and \(f(x) = bx + c\) is a linear function (a straight line), not a quadratic one. \(b\) and \(c\) may be zero.

blocks.caption: Reading a, b and c (our examples; the sign goes with the number)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Always rewrite the function in the order \(ax^{2} + bx + c\) before reading the coefficients. For \(f(x) = 6 - x - x^{2}\), the order is \(-x^{2} - x + 6\), so \(a = -1\), \(b = -1\), \(c = 6\).
The sign of \(a\) is the most important single piece of information: in 3.1.1 we will see that it decides whether the graph opens upward or downward.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A quadratic function has the standard form \(f(x) = ax^{2} + bx + c\), with \(a, b, c\) real and \(a \ne 0\).
2. Its degree is 2: the highest power of \(x\) is 2.
3. \(a\) is the leading coefficient, \(b\) the coefficient of \(x\), \(c\) the constant term.
4. Write the terms in the order \(x^{2}\), \(x\), constant before reading \(a\), \(b\), \(c\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Dropping the sign: in \(f(x) = -x^{2} - 2x + 3\), \(a = -1\) and \(b = -2\), not \(1\) and \(2\).
2. Reading the coefficients from an unordered expression: in \(6 - x - x^{2}\), \(a\) is not 6.
3. Calling \(f(x) = 0x^{2} + 5x + 1\) quadratic: with \(a = 0\) it is linear.
